evidence_quotes.quote: Este artigo tem por objetivos analisar a noção da água com bem comum construída por populações rurais, investigar as bases em que essa concepção se fundamenta e, por fim, avaliar os impactos que a centralização da gestão da água causa sobre as culturas locais na gestão de recursos hídricos.

Córregos são águas das comunidades, porque o coletivo das famílias se serve delas e em conjunto regulam suas usanças. Já os rios e ribeirões são considerados de domínio público, porque há muitos moradores que os utilizam, poluindo com sabão, dejetos, lida de animais, tornando difícil a regulação comunitária; essa gestão compete ao Estado.

Esse estudo é fruto de pesquisa realizada entre 2002 e 2009 em comunidades rurais de três regiões de Minas Gerais: os vales do rio São Francisco, do rio Jequitinhonha e a Serra da Mantiqueira. Essa escolha buscou diversidade de ambientes e de oferta de água (abundância ou escassez). Ao total foram pesquisadas dezoito localidades.

Foram usados dois roteiros de pesquisa: um para observação do ambiente, partilha da terra e sistemas de lavouras; outro para entrevista, bastante aberto, buscava informações sobre família, comunidade, terra e água.

Por um lado, o Instituto Estadual de Florestas impunha a conservação de mananciais por meio da lei, da polícia florestal e das multas, apesar de constantemente desafiados pelas famílias. Por outro, o caso de comunidades rurais que, apoiados pelo Centro de Agricultura Alternativa Vicente Nica e baseadas na classificação cultural de qualidade de água, elegeram a conservação de nascentes como principal ação relacionada aos recursos hídricos.

No Brasil qual espaço político e cultural a Lei das Águas – participativa, mas excludente – e o mercado – que concebe água como bem econômico – deixarão para a pequena regulação comunitária? Quase que somente o espaço subalterno do conflito, pois se configuram situações onde a água bem econômico tende a ser hegemônica: não só está fundamentada na Lei das Águas, como também a institui.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper is an anthropological/ethnoecological study of rural peasant conceptions, cultural classifications, and customary common-pool management of raw natural water resources (springs/nascentes, streams/córregos, and rivers/rios used for domestic drinking, livestock, and farming) and headwater spring conservation across 18 rural communities in Minas Gerais. No water supply service, piped network, utility, rural service scheme, or sanitation service is studied (Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), Criterion 2 itself would pass because the paper examines customary community water-governance norms ('normas costumeiras', 'gestão comunitária das águas'), state forestry policing/fines for headwater conservation (Instituto Estadual de Florestas), and macro-level tensions with Brazil's Water Law ('Lei das Águas'); however, the overall study would still be excluded under Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 because it examines raw natural water resources rather than water or sanitation service access (so plain_criterion2_decision = 'exclude'). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, c2 is 'no': the paper does not examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements for service connection, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Instead, it focuses on peasant moral/religious reciprocity norms over natural springs, environmental forestry conservation of headwaters, and unanalysed macro-governance commentary on the Lei das Águas in the closing section.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. The paper reports primary qualitative empirical research conducted between 2002 and 2009 across 18 rural communities in three regions of Minas Gerais using environmental observations, open-ended interviews with farming families, and community-wide meetings.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The paper does not report outcomes on household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, service continuity, affordability, or service exclusion; instead, it describes peasant cosmological/moral norms around raw water ('água viva' vs. 'água morta', 'água pequena' vs. 'água grande'), spring-sharing ethics, perceived reductions in rainfall and river flow from upstream irrigation/dams/deforestation, and community fencing/revegetation of 26 springs.
criterion_notes.c5: Unclear. The rural community/bairro rural unit of analysis, study regions (18 localities in Minas Gerais), and qualitative field-research design are clearly identified in text, although Quadro 1 (sample details) and Quadro 2 are omitted/blank in the PDF text extraction and no water/sanitation service-access exposure or outcome is identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in Portuguese, which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Qualitative field study (ethnographic / socio-anthropological environmental observations, open-ended household interviews, and community meetings conducted 2002–2009)
population_and_sample: Peasant farming families (famílias de lavradores) across 18 rural communities / neighborhoods (bairros rurais) in three regions of Minas Gerais (São Francisco valley, Jequitinhonha valley, and Serra da Mantiqueira); unit of analysis is the rural community / bairro rural (household counts in Quadro 1 are not rendered in the PDF)
exposure: Customary peasant moral norms and community conceptions of raw natural water as a common good (bem comum / dádiva), headwater spring conservation rules, and macro-level commentary on statutory water-resource management
outcome: Cultural classifications of raw water quality (água viva/corrente vs. água morta/parada; água pequena vs. água grande), customary spring-sharing practices, and headwater spring revegetation/conservation (no water or sanitation service-access outcome)
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Drawing on qualitative fieldwork across 18 rural communities in Minas Gerais (2002–2009), the paper examines peasant cultural representations of raw natural water as a divine gift and common good, local ethnoecological classifications of springs, streams, and rivers, and headwater spring conservation, rather than household or community water supply or sanitation service access (c1 = no, c4 = no). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it also examines no legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access, offering only descriptions of customary moral reciprocity around natural springs, forestry conservation policing, and unanalysed closing remarks on Brazil's Lei das Águas (c2 = no; under the plain wording of Criterion 2, community water governance would satisfy c2 itself, but the study remains excluded for failing c1 and c4).
